cards.h: Law is how environment policy bites
cards.b:
Prelims asks the year and subject of each Act and the NGT’s powers. Mains asks whether Indian environmental law is effective.

Learn the constitutional base, the main Acts and the principles courts use.

Article 48A (DPSP, added by the 42nd Amendment 1976): the State shall protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife. Article 51A(g): a Fundamental Duty of every citizen. Article 21: courts read a right to a healthy environment into the right to life (Subhash Kumar v State of Bihar, 1991).

The 42nd Amendment also moved forests and wild animals to the Concurrent List (Entries 17A, 17B). Article 253 lets Parliament legislate to implement treaties.

• Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972
  • Water Act 1974; Water Cess Act 1977
  • Forest (Conservation) Act 1980
  • Air Act 1981
  • Environment (Protection) Act 1986: the umbrella law, passed after Bhopal (December 1984) and the Stockholm Conference.
  • Public Liability Insurance Act 1991
  • Biological Diversity Act 2002
  • Forest Rights Act 2006; NGT Act 2010

It gives the Centre power to set standards, restrict industry locations, issue directions and make rules such as the EIA, CRZ, noise and waste rules. Offences carry penalties.

Under the Jan Vishwas Act 2023, many jail terms in the EPA were replaced by penalties (from ₹10,000 up to ₹15 lakh), with adjudicating officers. Supporters see ease of business; critics see weaker deterrence.

Polluter pays, precautionary principle and public trust doctrine were all accepted in Indian law. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996) and the Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996) cases built these in. M.C. Mehta v Kamal Nath (1997) applied the public trust doctrine.

In M.C. Mehta (Oleum gas leak, 1986) the Court created absolute liability for hazardous industries, going beyond the old strict liability of Rylands v Fletcher.

The National Green Tribunal Act 2010 created the NGT, replacing the National Environment Tribunal (1995) and the National Environment Appellate Authority (1997). The Principal Bench is in Delhi, with benches at Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai.

India became one of the few countries with a specialist green tribunal. The chair is a retired Supreme Court judge or High Court Chief Justice, along with judicial and expert members.

The NGT hears civil cases involving a substantial environmental question under seven Acts: Water, Water Cess, Forest Conservation, Air, Environment Protection, Public Liability Insurance and Biological Diversity. It does not hear cases under the Wildlife Protection Act, the Indian Forest Act 1927 or local state tree laws.

It follows natural justice, not the strict Civil Procedure Code, aims to decide within six months, can award compensation and restoration, and its orders can be appealed to the Supreme Court within 90 days.

The NGT has acted on the Ganga, Yamuna, Delhi air quality and illegal mining. Critics point to its limited jurisdiction, vacancies, weak execution, and a Supreme Court ruling that it also has some suo motu power (2021).

Executive influence over appointments and the narrow list of Acts are a regular concern.

In M.K. Ranjitsinh v Union of India (2024) the Supreme Court recognised a right to be free from the adverse effects of climate change as part of Articles 14 and 21.

Local bodies have a role under the 11th Schedule (Article 243G). States also have their own pollution control boards under the Water and Air Acts.

Mains-style: “Assess the role of the NGT in environmental governance. What are its limitations?” Structure: origin; jurisdiction; principles; notable orders; limits (narrow Acts, enforcement, vacancies); reforms.

Mains-style: “Polluter pays and precautionary principles: how have Indian courts used them?”

Prelims tip: NGT Act 2010; Article 48A (42nd Amendment); EPA 1986 after Bhopal; NGT excludes the Wildlife Act.
